answers.transcript:
Okay, so I want to talk about some advice from my chemistry teacher.
He said me study a little every day, don't wait the last week before the exam.
He told me this in the lycee, when I am sixteen years old.
In that time I was studying only in the night before the exam.
Sometimes I got good notes but sometimes I forgetted everything after two week.
After his advice I started to study one hour every day and it was more easy.
My results become better in one term, especially in the chemistry and the physics.
Now I am at the university and I use the same method for all my lessons.
For example I repeat my notes in the same evening, not after two weeks.
I think this is the best advice what somebody gave me, because it is simple and everybody can do it.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: The advice, who it came from, when it came and how it helps today come in sequence, so all four points on the card are addressed, but each point closes in one sentence. Transitions follow the pattern "After his advice", "Now", "For example", and the final two sentences repeat the same idea.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: Vocabulary describing study habits is very narrow: study, exam, notes, results repeat. The advice itself does not land in a matching form either; "notes" is used in the Turkish sense of "grade".
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: Verb pattern errors (said me, wait the last week), an irregular verb (forgetted), tense agreement (when I am sixteen, results become better), comparison (more easy) and a relative pronoun error (the best advice what) appear in most sentences. Structures are simple, with no complex structure.

answers.what_would_lift_it: Tell one single instance where the advice worked — which exam, what changed — because at present the benefit is summarised with "my results become better". In the language, first fix basic forms such as "said me" and "forgetted".

answers.transcript:
The advice I want to talk about is something my chemistry teacher told me when I was sixteen years old.
He said, don't study everything in the last week, study a little bit every day and repeat the subject before you forget it.
At that time I was a typical student who was doing all the work in the night before the exam, sometimes until four o'clock.
And the problem was, my marks were okay but after two weeks I couldn't remember nothing from the subject.
So I decided to take his advice on board, and I started to study one hour every evening, even when there was no exam.
It was not easy at the beginning, but after two or three weeks it became a habit.
My results in chemistry and physics got much better in one term, and I was much less stressed before the exams.
Now I am at the university and I am still using the same system, I repeat my lecture notes in the same evening.
Of course it is easier said than done, and sometimes I skip two or three days.
But this advice stayed with me for years, and I think it is the most useful sentence that somebody said me.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: The advice is first reported, then compared with the before and after; this structure carries the narrative and all four points are developed. The flow becomes mechanical: sections open in the same pattern with "At that time", "So I decided", "Now I am".
why_this_band.lexical_resource: There is vocabulary to carry the topic (take his advice on board, easier said than done, became a habit, lecture notes), and meaning is never closed off. Phrasing flattens in reporting the advice: "repeat the subject", "study a little bit every day".
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: A relative clause, the past continuous, reported speech and time clauses are controlled; more than two-thirds of sentences are error-free. The remaining errors sit in a narrow set: preposition (in the night before), a double negative (couldn't remember nothing), verb pattern (somebody said me).

answers.what_would_lift_it: Make the moment the advice paid off concrete: describe a single exam instead of "my results got much better". In the language, fixing the "say something to somebody" pattern and the double negative is enough; the rest of the structure is already solid.

answers.transcript:
So the advice I keep coming back to came from my chemistry teacher, of all people, when I was about sixteen.
What he said was, don't study more, study sooner. Or, well, what he actually meant was go over something the same evening you learn it, before you've had a chance to forget it.
Which sounds obvious, I know. But at that age I was a classic crammer. I'd do nothing for a month and then pull two all-nighters before the exam.
And the marks weren't even that bad, which was sort of the problem, because it meant I had no real reason to change anything. It all went in one ear and out the other about a fortnight later.
For whatever reason that particular sentence stuck with me, though, and I did actually take it on board. An hour most evenings, exam or no exam.
By the end of that term my grades in chemistry and physics had gone up noticeably and, more to the point, I wasn't in a permanent state of panic.
It's stood me in good stead ever since. I'm at university now and I still go over my lecture notes the same day, even if it's only twenty minutes on the bus home.
It's easier said than done when you're shattered, obviously, and there are weeks where it slips completely. But it's probably the single most useful thing anyone's ever told me, and it took him about ten seconds to say it.

why_this_band.fluency_coherence: The narrative builds its own order, and stating the advice first and then opening up why it worked carries the flow; the closing ties back by returning to how short the advice was. There is one self-correction ("Or, well, what he actually meant was"), the kind that eight lines allow.
why_this_band.lexical_resource: Less common items are plentiful and in place: of all people, a classic crammer, pull two all-nighters, in one ear and out the other, stuck with me, take it on board, more to the point, stood me in good stead, easier said than done, shattered.
why_this_band.grammatical_range_accuracy: Structural range is wide: the past perfect (my grades had gone up), "before you've had a chance to forget it", a concessive clause with "even if it's only twenty minutes", elliptical structures (An hour most evenings). There is no countable error.

answers.what_would_lift_it: This is on target; for the next level up, the weeks where the advice does not hold also need to be opened up — "there are weeks where it slips" is left in a single sentence. There is nothing left to do in the language.
